distractors.text: States of $C$ are transient if some state outside $C$ can reach $C$, since the chain may never return.
distractors.misconception: lets entry from outside decide the type of the states inside

distractors.text: A closed class can contain both recurrent and transient states if its transition probabilities are unequal.
distractors.misconception: forgets that recurrence is a class property

distractors.text: States of $C$ are recurrent only if the whole chain is irreducible, so that every state is reachable.
distractors.misconception: thinks recurrence of a class needs irreducibility of the whole chain

explanation: A finite closed class cannot be left and cannot be avoided forever, so every state in it is revisited infinitely often: it is recurrent (indeed positive recurrent). Periodicity and states outside $C$ do not matter.

stem: In an irreducible positive recurrent Markov chain, the expected hitting time $E_i[T_j]$ of a state $j$, starting from a state $i$, is:
correct: Finite for every pair of states $i$ and $j$.
Finite whichever starting state $i$ and target state $j$ are chosen.

distractors.text: Finite only when $i=j$, and infinite when $i\ne j$.
distractors.misconception: mixes up the return time with the hitting time of a different state

distractors.text: Equal to $1/\pi_j$ for every starting state $i$, including $i\ne j$.
distractors.misconception: applies the formula for the mean return time to hitting times from other states

distractors.text: Finite only if the chain is aperiodic, since periodic chains avoid some states at some times.
distractors.misconception: thinks periodicity can make hitting times infinite

distractors.text: Finite only if the state space is finite, since infinite chains can wander away.
distractors.misconception: thinks positive recurrence needs a finite state space

distractors.text: Infinite for at least one pair $i\ne j$ whenever the chain has more than two states.
distractors.misconception: invents infinite hitting times in a positive recurrent chain

explanation: Irreducible plus positive recurrent gives finite mean hitting times between every pair of states: from $i$ the chain reaches $j$ in finite expected time and then also returns in finite expected time. Periodicity and the size of the state space do not change this.

stem: A chain has exactly two closed communicating classes, each positive recurrent, with stationary distributions $\pi^{(1)}$ and $\pi^{(2)}$ (each supported on its own class). Which statement is correct?
correct: Every mixture $\alpha\pi^{(1)}+(1-\alpha)\pi^{(2)}$ with $0\le\alpha\le1$ is stationary, so the stationary distribution is not unique.
There are infinitely many stationary distributions, namely all convex combinations of $\pi^{(1)}$ and $\pi^{(2)}$.

distractors.text: The stationary distribution is unique, because each closed class has its own unique stationary distribution.
distractors.misconception: assumes uniqueness within a class gives uniqueness for the whole chain

distractors.text: There are exactly two stationary distributions, $\pi^{(1)}$ and $\pi^{(2)}$, and no others.
distractors.misconception: forgets that mixtures of stationary distributions are stationary

distractors.text: There is no stationary distribution, because the chain is not irreducible.
distractors.misconception: thinks irreducibility is needed for existence

distractors.text: The only stationary distribution is the equal mixture $\tfrac12\pi^{(1)}+\tfrac12\pi^{(2)}$.
distractors.misconception: singles out one mixture without a reason

distractors.text: Only the distribution supported on the larger class is stationary, because the chain eventually settles there.
distractors.misconception: confuses stationarity with where the chain ends up

explanation: If $\pi^{(1)}P=\pi^{(1)}$ and $\pi^{(2)}P=\pi^{(2)}$, then any convex combination also satisfies $\pi P=\pi$. Uniqueness needs a single closed class.

stem: A gambler starts with $i\ge1$ units and wins each round with probability $p>\tfrac12$ (loses with probability $q=1-p$). There is no upper target. With $r=q/p$, the probability that he is eventually ruined is:
correct: $r^{\,i}=(q/p)^{i}$, which is less than 1.
$(q/p)^{i}$: the chance that the walk ever goes down by $i$ levels.

distractors.text: $1$, because a game with no target continues until the gambler is ruined.
distractors.misconception: assumes ruin is certain when there is no upper barrier

distractors.text: $q^{\,i}$, the probability of losing $i$ rounds in a row.
distractors.misconception: counts only the direct path of $i$ consecutive losses

distractors.text: $1-(q/p)^{i}$, the probability that he is never ruined.
distractors.misconception: reports the survival probability instead of the ruin probability

distractors.text: $i\,q/p$, growing linearly with the starting fortune.
distractors.misconception: makes the ruin probability grow with the fortune, and it can exceed 1

distractors.text: $q/p$, whatever the starting fortune $i$ is.
distractors.misconception: ignores the dependence on the starting fortune

explanation: Ruin from $i$ means reaching $0$ before $\infty$, the limit $N\to\infty$ of $1-(1-r^i)/(1-r^N)$ with $r<1$, giving $r^i$.

stem: $X\sim\mathrm{Exp}(a)$ and $Y\sim\mathrm{Exp}(b)$ are independent. Which statement about $\min(X,Y)$ is correct?
correct: $\min(X,Y)\sim\mathrm{Exp}(a+b)$, and the minimum is independent of which of $X$ and $Y$ is smaller.
It is $\mathrm{Exp}(a+b)$, and $P(X<Y)=a/(a+b)$ whatever the value of the minimum happens to be.

distractors.text: It is $\mathrm{Exp}\big(ab/(a+b)\big)$, a harmonic-type combination of the two rates, independent of $\{X<Y\}$.
distractors.misconception: combines the rates with a product over a sum instead of adding them

distractors.text: It is $\mathrm{Exp}(\max(a,b))$, because the faster clock always rings first, and so decides the race.
distractors.misconception: thinks the faster clock always wins

distractors.text: It is $\mathrm{Exp}\big((a+b)/2\big)$, the average of the two rates, and independent of $\{X<Y\}$.
distractors.misconception: averages the rates instead of adding them

distractors.text: It is $\mathrm{Exp}(a+b)$, but $X$ is more likely to be the smaller one when the minimum is small.
distractors.misconception: thinks the identity of the winner depends on the time of the first ring

distractors.text: It is a Gamma random variable with shape 2, being the first of two exponential waiting times.
distractors.misconception: mixes up a minimum of two clocks with a sum of two waiting times

explanation: $P(\min>t)=P(X>t)P(Y>t)=e^{-(a+b)t}$, so the minimum is $\mathrm{Exp}(a+b)$. Also $P(X<Y\mid\min=t)=a/(a+b)$ for all $t$.

stem: Given $N(t)=n$ in a Poisson process, the $n$ arrival times in $[0,t]$ are distributed as:
correct: The order statistics of $n$ independent $\mathrm{Uniform}(0,t)$ random variables.
The sorted values of $n$ independent random points chosen uniformly in $[0,t]$.

distractors.text: $n$ independent $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ random variables, sorted into increasing order.
distractors.misconception: carries over the interarrival law to the arrival times

distractors.text: Equally spaced points $t/(n+1),\,2t/(n+1),\dots,nt/(n+1)$, with no randomness left.
distractors.misconception: thinks conditioning on the count removes all randomness

distractors.text: The first $n$ partial sums of independent $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ gaps, without any conditioning on $t$.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the conditioning changes the joint law

distractors.text: $n$ independent $\mathrm{Uniform}(0,t)$ variables, but with the largest one fixed equal to $t$.
distractors.misconception: pins the last arrival to the end of the interval

distractors.text: A random set whose joint law depends on the rate $\lambda$ through the factor $\lambda^{n}$.
distractors.misconception: thinks the conditional law still depends on the rate

explanation: Given the number of points, a Poisson process places them like independent uniform points; the rate $\lambda$ drops out.

stem: For a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$, times $s<t$ and counts $m\le n$, $P\big(N(t)=n\mid N(s)=m\big)$ equals:
correct: $e^{-\lambda(t-s)}\dfrac{\big(\lambda(t-s)\big)^{n-m}}{(n-m)!}$.
The $\mathrm{Poisson}\big(\lambda(t-s)\big)$ probability of exactly $n-m$ arrivals in $(s,t]$.

distractors.text: $e^{-\lambda t}\dfrac{(\lambda t)^{n}}{n!}$, the unconditional probability that $N(t)=n$.
distractors.misconception: ignores the information that $N(s)=m$

distractors.text: $e^{-\lambda t}\dfrac{(\lambda t)^{n-m}}{(n-m)!}$, with the mean based on the whole interval $(0,t]$.
distractors.misconception: uses the wrong interval length for the remaining arrivals

distractors.text: $e^{-\lambda(t-s)}\dfrac{\big(\lambda(t-s)\big)^{n}}{n!}$, ignoring the $m$ arrivals already seen.
distractors.misconception: forgets that only $n-m$ more arrivals are needed

distractors.text: $\binom{n}{m}(s/t)^{m}(1-s/t)^{n-m}$, the binomial probability of the split.
distractors.misconception: gives the reversed conditional probability $P(N(s)=m\mid N(t)=n)$

distractors.text: $1$ if $n=m+1$ and $0$ otherwise, since arrivals occur one at a time.
distractors.misconception: confuses ordinary arrivals with a single arrival per interval

explanation: Independent stationary increments: given $N(s)=m$, the count in $(s,t]$ is still $\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda(t-s))$, and we need exactly $n-m$ of them.

stem: A finite continuous-time chain has an absorbing state that can be reached from every other state. The time until absorption, starting from a transient state, is:
correct: Finite with probability 1, and a sum of exponential holding times along a random path of states.
A phase-type random variable: a random sum of independent exponential holding times.

distractors.text: Exponential with rate equal to the exit rate of the starting state.
distractors.misconception: takes the first holding time for the whole time to absorption

distractors.text: Gamma distributed, because each visited state contributes one exponential holding time.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the rates and the number of steps are random

distractors.text: Geometric, since the chain either gets absorbed or does not at each jump.
distractors.misconception: mixes up continuous time with a discrete number of jumps

distractors.text: Infinite with positive probability, because the chain may keep moving among the transient states forever.
distractors.misconception: thinks a finite chain can avoid absorption forever

distractors.text: Uniformly distributed between the shortest and the longest possible holding times.
distractors.misconception: replaces a sum of exponentials by a uniform law

explanation: Each visit contributes an independent exponential holding time, and the number and identity of visited states is random. Absorption is certain in a finite chain with an accessible absorbing state.

stem: In equilibrium, an M/M/1 queue with arrival rate $\lambda$ and service rate $\mu>\lambda$ has a departure process that is:
correct: A Poisson process with rate $\lambda$, the same as the arrival rate (Burke's theorem).
Poisson with the same rate $\lambda$ as the arrival process, whatever $\mu>\lambda$ is.

distractors.text: A Poisson process with rate $\mu$, the rate at which the server works.
distractors.misconception: uses the service rate, though the server is idle part of the time

distractors.text: A Poisson process with rate $\mu-\lambda$, the spare capacity of the server.
distractors.misconception: uses the spare capacity as the departure rate

distractors.text: Periodic, with departures spaced $1/\mu$ apart, since the server always works at full speed.
distractors.misconception: thinks departures are regular because service is exponential

distractors.text: Not a Poisson process, because the service times are exponential rather than the arrivals.
distractors.misconception: thinks a Poisson input cannot give a Poisson output

distractors.text: A Poisson process with rate $\lambda\mu/(\lambda+\mu)$, a compromise between the two rates.
distractors.misconception: invents a harmonic-type combination of the rates

explanation: Burke: the stationary M/M/1 queue is reversible, so its departure process has the same law as its arrival process, namely Poisson($\lambda$), whatever $\mu>\lambda$ is.

stem: Let $F$ be the distribution function of the interarrival times of a renewal process and $m(t)=E[N(t)]$. Conditioning on the first renewal gives:
correct: $m(t)=F(t)+\displaystyle\int_0^t m(t-s)\,dF(s)$, the renewal equation.
$m(t)=F(t)+E\big[m(t-S_1);\,S_1\le t\big]$, with $S_1$ the first renewal time.

distractors.text: $m(t)=t/\mu$ for every $t\ge0$, exactly, whatever the gap distribution.
distractors.misconception: uses the asymptotic rate as an exact formula

distractors.text: $m(t)=F(t)^{2}$, the probability that two renewals occur by time $t$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the mean with the probability of two renewals

distractors.text: $m(t)=\displaystyle\int_0^t m(t-s)\,dF(s)$, without the term for the first renewal itself.
distractors.misconception: forgets to count the first renewal

distractors.text: $m(t)=1-F(t)$, the probability that no renewal has happened by time $t$.
distractors.misconception: gives the probability of no renewal instead of the mean count

distractors.text: $m(t)=F(t)+m(t)$, since after the first renewal the process restarts.
distractors.misconception: writes a tautology and cannot be solved

explanation: If the first renewal is at $s\le t$, we count it (1) and then expect $m(t-s)$ more; otherwise there are none. Averaging over $S_1\sim F$ gives $m(t)=\int_0^t(1+m(t-s))\,dF(s)=F(t)+\int_0^tm(t-s)\,dF(s)$.

stem: In a subcritical branching process ($m<1$, $Z_0=1$), the expected total number of individuals ever born, $E\big[\sum_{n\ge0}Z_n\big]$, is:
correct: $1/(1-m)$, the sum of the geometric series $\sum_n m^{\,n}$, root included, for $m<1$.
$\sum_{n\ge0}m^{\,n}=1/(1-m)$, which is finite because $m<1$ for a subcritical process.

distractors.text: $m/(1-m)$, which leaves out the initial individual from the total count of the population.
distractors.misconception: forgets the initial individual

distractors.text: Infinite, because the line may continue for many generations before it dies out.
distractors.misconception: thinks a subcritical population can have infinite expected progeny

distractors.text: $1/m$, the reciprocal of the offspring mean, which exceeds 1 when $m<1$.
distractors.misconception: inverts the offspring mean

distractors.text: $1+m+m^{2}$, the sum over the first three generations only, and nothing after that.
distractors.misconception: truncates the geometric series

distractors.text: $(1-m)^{-2}$, the square of the reciprocal of $1-m$, as for a double series.
distractors.misconception: squares the sum of the geometric series

explanation: $E[Z_n]=m^n$, so the expected total is the geometric series $\sum_n m^n=1/(1-m)$ for $m<1$ (it counts the root).

stem: Let $m>1$ and assume the offspring law has finite variance. The martingale $W_n=Z_n/m^{n}$ then:
correct: Converges almost surely to a limit $W$ that is positive exactly on the event that the population survives.
Has a limit $W$ with $E[W]=1$ and $W=0$ on extinction, so $Z_n$ grows like $m^{n}$ on survival.

distractors.text: Converges to $1$ almost surely, so $Z_n\approx m^{n}$ on every sample path.
distractors.misconception: ignores randomness and extinction

distractors.text: Converges to $0$ almost surely, because $Z_n$ is eventually smaller than $m^{n}$.
distractors.misconception: confuses a martingale with mean 1 with a process that dies out

distractors.text: Does not converge, because the fluctuations of $Z_n$ are of the same order as $m^{n}$.
distractors.misconception: thinks the relative fluctuations never settle down

distractors.text: Converges to a limit $W$ that is positive with probability 1, since a supercritical population cannot die out.
distractors.misconception: forgets that extinction has positive probability

distractors.text: Converges to $m$ almost surely, since each individual has $m$ children on average.
distractors.misconception: mixes up the limit with the offspring mean

explanation: $W_n$ is a non-negative martingale bounded in $L^2$ when the variance is finite, so $W_n\to W$ with $E[W]=1$. On extinction $W=0$; on survival $W>0$ (Kesten-Stigum).

stem: For the simple symmetric random walk $S_n$ started at $0$, let $T$ be the first time $|S_n|=a$. Applying optional stopping to the martingale $S_n^2-n$ gives $E[T]=$:
correct: $a^{2}$, the square of the distance to the boundary.
$a^2$, because $E[S_T^2]=a^2$ and $E[S_T^2-T]=0$.

distractors.text: $a$, the distance to the boundary.
distractors.misconception: mixes up a distance with a time

distractors.text: $2a$, the width of the interval $[-a,a]$.
distractors.misconception: uses the width of the interval

distractors.text: $a^{2}/2$, half of the squared distance.
distractors.misconception: introduces a spurious factor of one half

distractors.text: $a^{2}+a$, the squared distance plus the distance.
distractors.misconception: adds an unjustified term

distractors.text: $\infty$, because the symmetric walk is recurrent.
distractors.misconception: thinks recurrence makes the exit time infinite

explanation: $S_T^2=a^2$ always, and $E[S_T^2-T]=0$ by optional stopping (justified since $T$ has finite mean and the increments are bounded), so $E[T]=a^2$.

stem: A non-negative martingale $(M_n)$ is given. Which statement is correct?
correct: It converges almost surely to a finite limit $M_\infty$, but $E[M_\infty]$ may be smaller than $E[M_0]$.
Almost sure convergence always holds, yet convergence in $L^1$ can fail.

distractors.text: It converges in $L^1$ as well, so $E[M_\infty]=E[M_0]$ always.
distractors.misconception: assumes convergence in mean from almost sure convergence

distractors.text: It converges to $0$ almost surely, since non-negative fair games are eventually ruined.
distractors.misconception: forgets that a constant is a non-negative martingale

distractors.text: It need not converge, because martingales are allowed to oscillate indefinitely.
distractors.misconception: forgets Doob's convergence theorem for non-negative martingales

distractors.text: It is bounded, because a non-negative fair game cannot grow without limit.
distractors.misconception: thinks a fair game is bounded

distractors.text: It converges almost surely only if it is bounded in $L^2$, and not otherwise.
distractors.misconception: treats a sufficient condition as necessary

explanation: Doob: non-negative martingales converge a.s. For $M_n=\prod_{k\le n}\xi_k$ with i.i.d. $\xi_k\in\{0,2\}$ equally likely, $M_n\to0$ a.s. while $E[M_n]=1$, so $L^1$ convergence fails.

stem: For the simple symmetric walk $S_n$ from $0$, let $T=\min\{n: S_n=1\}$. Then $T<\infty$ almost surely and $S_T=1$, yet $E[S_T]=1\ne0=E[S_0]$. Why does optional stopping not apply?
correct: $T$ is not bounded and the stopped martingale is not uniformly integrable; indeed $E[T]=\infty$.
The conditions fail: $T$ has infinite mean and $(S_{n\wedge T})$ is not uniformly integrable.

distractors.text: $S_n$ is not a martingale, because its increments are $\pm1$.
distractors.misconception: thinks bounded increments rule out the martingale property

distractors.text: $T$ is not a stopping time, since it depends on the whole future of the walk.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the event $\{T\le n\}$ is decided by the path up to time $n$

distractors.text: $T$ is infinite with positive probability, so $S_T$ is not defined on a set of positive probability.
distractors.misconception: contradicts the premise that $T<\infty$ almost surely

distractors.text: Optional stopping applies, so $E[S_T]=0$, and the value $1$ must come from an error in the argument.
distractors.misconception: believes the theorem holds without conditions

distractors.text: The theorem requires $M$ to be non-negative, and the walk $S_n$ takes negative values.
distractors.misconception: invents non-negativity as the missing condition

explanation: The stopped walk $S_{n\wedge T}$ has $E=0$ for every $n$ but converges to $1$ a.s.: mass escapes to $-\infty$ with vanishing probability, so it is not uniformly integrable and $E[T]=\infty$.

stem: Let $(X_n)$ be a Markov chain on a finite state space with transition matrix $P$, and $h$ a function on the states. The process $h(X_n)$ is a martingale exactly when:
correct: $h(i)=\sum_j p_{ij}h(j)$ for every state $i$, so that one step of the chain leaves $h$ unchanged on average.
$h$ is harmonic for the chain: $Ph=h$, with $h$ written as a column vector.

distractors.text: $\sum_i h(i)=1$ and $h(i)\ge0$ for every state $i$.
distractors.misconception: confuses a harmonic function with a probability vector

distractors.text: $h(i)\ge\sum_j p_{ij}h(j)$ for every state $i$, with strict inequality somewhere.
distractors.misconception: describes a strict supermartingale

distractors.text: $hP=h$, with $h$ written as a row vector, that is $h$ is a stationary distribution.
distractors.misconception: multiplies on the wrong side, confusing harmonic functions with stationary vectors

distractors.text: $h$ is constant on each communicating class, and nowhere else is the condition met.
distractors.misconception: thinks harmonic functions are always constant on classes

distractors.text: The chain is symmetric, so that $p_{ij}=p_{ji}$ for all pairs of states.
distractors.misconception: adds a symmetry condition that is not needed

explanation: $E[h(X_{n+1})\mid X_n=i]=\sum_jp_{ij}h(j)$, so $h(X_n)$ is a martingale iff this equals $h(i)$ for every $i$. Hitting probabilities are the standard non-constant examples.
